pg007_n0006: This textbook, Mathematics for Secondary Schools Form two, is written specifically for Form Two students in the United Republic of Tanzania.
pg007_n0007: The book is prepared in accordance with the twenty twenty-three Mathematics Syllabus for Ordinary Secondary Education, Form one to Form four, issued by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology.
pg007_n0008: It is a revised edition of Basic Mathematics for Secondary Schools Student’s Book Form Two that was published in twenty twenty-one in accordance with the two thousand five syllabus issued by the then, Ministry of Education and Vocational Training, M O E V T.
pg007_n0010: The textbook consists of eight chapters, namely: Rates and variations, Congruence, Similarity, Algebra, Exponents and radicals, Logarithms, Sets, and Trigonometry.
pg007_n0011: In addition to the contents, each chapter contains activities, illustrations, projects, and exercises.
pg007_n0012: You are encouraged to do all the activities, and questions in the exercises.
pg007_n0013: This will enhance your understanding and development of the intended competencies for this level.

pg008_n0012: Understanding rates and variations is essential for grasping how quantities change in relation to each other.
pg008_n0013: Some variables are interdependent, meaning a change in one affects the others.
pg008_n0014: Many real-life situations involve such relationships.
pg008_n0015: In this chapter, you will describe the concepts of rates and variations, explain the types of variations, and solve problems on rates and variations.
pg008_n0016: The competencies developed will enable you to solve real-life challenges such as finding shopping deals, assessing fuel efficiency, or predicting data trends in fields like economics, science, engineering, and many other applications.

pg012_n0037: Variation is a relationship where a change in one quantity leads to a proportional change in the other.
pg012_n0038: It allows for the exploration of connections between two or more quantities.
pg012_n0039: The four basic types of variations are direct, inverse, joint, and combined.
pg013_n0005: Direct variation is a relationship between two variables where one variable is a constant multiple of the other.
pg013_n0006: In other words, if one variable increases or decreases, the other variable changes proportionally in the same direction.
pg013_n0008: This type of variation is useful for understanding how changes in one variable affect another in a directly proportional manner.
pg013_n0010: Engage in Activity one point three to explore the application of direct variation in real life.
pg013_n0012: If y is directly proportional to x, it can be written as y is proportional to x, where the proportional to symbol is a symbol of proportionality.
pg013_n0013: The corresponding mathematical equation connecting x and y is formed by introducing a proportionality constant k, and replaces proportional to with an equal sign to get, y equals k x.
pg013_n0015: For instance, if y varies directly as the square of x, then y is proportional to x squared and the corresponding equation is y equals k x squared, where k is the constant of proportionality.
pg013_n0017: For any two pairs of quantities x and y, say, open parenthesis x one, y one close parenthesis and open parenthesis x two, y two close parenthesis, two equations y one equals k x one squared and y two equals k x two squared are obtained.
pg013_n0018: This implies that k equals y one over x one squared equals y two over x two squared.
pg013_n0019: So, it is said that x and y vary directly if the ratios of the values of y to the values of x are proportional.
pg013_n0021: If x and y are any two quantities that are in direct variation, then y equals k x.
pg013_n0022: The nature of the equation y equals k x is a straight line passing through the origin, where k represents the gradient, slope, of the line.
pg013_n0023: Figure one point one shows the relation y is proportional to x for k equals one.

A red straight line with arrowheads extends from the lower left to the upper right and passes exactly through the origin, showing a positive linear relationship of direct variation, y proportional to x, specifically the line y equals x.
pg013_n0025: Figure one point one: Graph of the relation y is proportional to x.
pg013_n0027: From Figure one point one, it can be observed that an increase, or decrease, in the quantity x results in a proportional increase, or decrease, in the quantity y, and vice versa.

pg016_n0005: A relationship between two or more variables is said to be an inverse variation if the value of one variable increases while the other value decreases, or vice versa.
pg016_n0006: Engage in Activity one point four to explore further inverse variations.
pg016_n0008: Quantities with an inverse variation relationship are said to be inversely proportional to each other.
pg016_n0009: In this case, the quantities vary inversely or in inverse proportion.
pg016_n0010: Inverse proportion is sometimes referred to as indirect proportion.
pg016_n0012: For example, the number of men employed to cultivate a farm and time taken to complete the work are inversely related.
pg016_n0013: Likewise, the time to travel to a certain place and the speed are inversely related.
pg016_n0015: Generally, if y has an inverse relationship with x, then y is proportional to the reciprocal of x.
pg016_n0017: y is proportional to one over x
pg016_n0019: The equation relating y and x is formed by introducing a constant of proportionality, k and replacing the symbol of proportionality with an equal sign, equals.
pg016_n0020: That is, the inverse variation between y and x becomes;
pg016_n0021: y equals k times one over x
pg016_n0023: If y varies inversely as the square of x, the equation connecting x and y is y equals k over x squared, or k equals y x squared.
pg016_n0025: A sketch of a relation y is proportional to one over x squared for k equals one is shown in Figure one point two.
pg016_n0026: Note that, the curve representing y equals k over x squared approaches both axes but does not touch them.
pg016_n0027: This is because at x equals zero the curve is undefined.

pg026_n0009: In fields like architecture, engineering and design, precise measurements and patterns are crucial.
pg026_n0010: Maintaining such patterns and measurements across objects and designs requires an understanding of the relationship between shapes and their properties.
pg026_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about postulates, proofs and theorems on congruence as well as the congruence of triangles.
pg026_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to solve problems such as determining the dimensions of sides of figures without taking actual measurements, designing and making objects of the same shapes and sizes such as worn-out parts.
pg026_n0017: Without knowledge of congruence industries would take longer time to produce objects of the same shape and size.
pg026_n0021: The term congruence is derived from the Latin word congruentia which means agree or fit together exactly.
pg026_n0022: Engage in Activity two point one to explore the characteristics of objects from real life situations which fit together.
pg026_n0025: Activity two point one: Exploring congruence of objects
pg026_n0029: Create a shape of your choice in M S Word, copy and paste it, then drag it on top of the original and observe.
pg026_n0032: Enlarge the original shape, overlap it with the copied shape, and note any changes.
pg026_n0035: Use real objects, for example, coins or books, to repeat task one, or two where necessary, and compare your observations.
pg026_n0037: In Activity two point one, one may have noticed that same objects matched exactly on top of each other.
pg026_n0038: This means that the objects have the same shape and size.
pg026_n0039: Two or more objects with such characteristics are called congruent figures.
pg026_n0043: Understanding postulates, theorems, and proofs is important for developing a solid foundation in mathematics.
pg026_n0044: These concepts form the basis for logical reasoning and they are used to validate mathematical ideas.
pg027_n0007: A postulate is a statement that is accepted as true without any proof.
pg027_n0008: These statements are universally accepted, self-evident and can form the basis for further reasoning and making arguments.
pg027_n0009: The following are examples of postulates.
pg027_n0013: A circle can be drawn with any centre and radius.
pg027_n0016: A straight line can be drawn from any point to any other point.
pg027_n0019: All right angles are equal to each other.
pg027_n0023: A theorem is an argument that has been proved to be true based on past established results, definitions or postulates.
pg027_n0024: The following are examples of theorems.
pg027_n0028: The sum of interior angles of a triangle is one hundred eighty degrees.
pg027_n0031: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides.
pg027_n0034: The sum of interior angles of a quadrilateral is three hundred sixty degrees.
pg027_n0038: A proof is a series of logical statements that are based on definitions, previously established facts, and postulates that may be used to conclude the truth of a mathematical argument.
pg027_n0039: The following are common procedures when undertaking a proof.
pg027_n0043: Draw a clearly labelled diagram to represent a problem.
pg027_n0044: Indicate all the information such as equal angles, parallel lines, and congruent segments.
pg027_n0047: Write down the given information based on the labels of the supporting figures.
pg027_n0050: State the argument which needs to be proved.
pg027_n0053: Where necessary, make additional constructions with dotted lines to make the proof clear.
pg027_n0060: Refer the figures you have planned to use in the proof.
pg027_n0063: Provide arguments with reasons based on the given information or established facts.
pg027_n0066: Start with statements whose validity are given or are obvious.
pg027_n0069: The final statement is the conclusion about what was supposed to be proved.
pg027_n0071: Engage in Activity two point two to explore more about postulates, proofs, and theorems.

pg067_n0007: Skills in solving problems systematically, logically, and making connections between variables are essential in daily life.
pg067_n0008: Such skills can be developed and applied by learning algebra.
pg067_n0009: In this chapter, you will learn about binary operations, quadratic expressions, and solving quadratic equations.
pg067_n0010: The competencies developed will enable you to solve daily life problems such as budgeting, comparing prices, planning for a journey and figuring proportions in cooking.
pg067_n0011: Also, algebra is useful in other subjects and fields such as science, engineering and technology and many other applications.
pg067_n0014: The role algebra plays in real life.
pg067_n0017: A binary operation is a rule for combining two quantities to produce a unique quantity from the same set.
pg067_n0018: It makes use of symbols that represent one or more operations.
pg067_n0020: The symbols used in binary operations are not standard, this means, they do not represent a specific operation.
pg067_n0021: A symbol may be used in a certain operation in an expression, and yet have a different meaning in another expression.
pg067_n0023: A binary operation may be denoted by symbols such as delta and star, depending on the instructions given for the operation.
pg067_n0025: The instructions may be given in words or by symbols.
pg067_n0026: Binary operations may involve the basic arithmetic operations such as addition, plus, subtraction, minus, multiplication, times, and division, divided by, depending on the given definition.

pg072_n0049: An expression whose highest exponent, degree, of the variable is two is called a quadratic expression.
pg072_n0051: The following are examples of quadratic expressions:
pg072_n0055: four z squared plus three, the highest exponent, or degree, of z is two.
pg072_n0058: six y squared plus y, the highest exponent of y is two.
pg072_n0061: three n squared minus two n plus one, the highest exponent of n is two.
pg072_n0063: In general, a quadratic expression has the form a x squared plus b x plus c, where a is not equal to zero and a, b, and c are real numbers.
pg072_n0064: The term a x squared is called the quadratic term, where a is the coefficient of x squared.
pg072_n0065: The term b x is called the linear term, middle term, where b is the coefficient of x and c is the constant term.
pg072_n0067: For example, in the quadratic expression four x squared minus six x plus seven, the coefficient of x squared is four, the coefficient of x is negative six and the constant is seven.

pg079_n0069: A quadratic equation is formed when a quadratic expression is equal to a specific value.

pg079_n0071: a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero.

pg079_n0073: There are also several methods for solving quadratic equations, including factorization, completing the square, and the general quadratic formula.
pg080_n0005: To solve quadratic equations by factorization, the following steps can be used:
pg080_n0008: Step one. Write the equation in standard form:
pg080_n0009: a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero.
pg080_n0011: Step two. Rewrite the quadratic expression a x squared plus b x plus c as a product of two linear factors.
pg080_n0013: Step three. Set each factor equal to zero and solve for x.
pg080_n0017: If a quadratic equation is expressed as a product of two linear factors, say open parenthesis x plus a close parenthesis open parenthesis x plus b close parenthesis equals zero, where a and b are constants, then either x plus a equals zero or x plus b equals zero or both factors are equal to zero.
pg080_n0018: This is called Zero factor theorem which states that, if a product of two or more factors is zero, then at least one of the factors must be zero.

pg083_n0063: Solving quadratic equations by completing the square
pg083_n0065: In the previous section, a method for solving quadratic equations by splitting the middle term was discussed.
pg083_n0066: However, not all quadratic equations can be factored.
pg083_n0067: For instance, in case of x squared plus 5 x plus 14 equals 0, no two whole numbers add to 5 and multiply to give 14.
pg083_n0068: For such equations, methods such as completing the square and quadratic formula can be used.
pg083_n0070: Completing the square is a technique used to solve quadratic equations by transforming the left-hand side of the equation into a perfect square.
pg083_n0071: The steps involved are demonstrated in the following examples.
pg083_n0076: What must be added to x squared plus 10 x to make the expression a perfect square?
pg083_n0080: The term to be added must be the square of half the coefficient of x.
pg083_n0082: Half of 10 is one half times 10 equals 5.
pg083_n0084: Therefore, 25 must be added to x squared plus 10 x to make it a perfect square.
pg084_n0007: What must be added to x squared minus five over two x to make it a perfect square?
pg084_n0011: The coefficient of x is negative five over two.
pg084_n0012: Half of negative five over two is one half times negative five over two equals negative five over four.
pg084_n0013: The square of negative five over four is twenty-five over sixteen.
pg084_n0014: Therefore, twenty-five over sixteen must be added to x squared minus five over two x to make it a perfect square.

pg096_n0040: There are three groups of exponents namely positive, negative, and zero exponents.
pg096_n0041: Simplification of the exponents are usually based on the four laws called multiplication, division, power, and zero power.
pg096_n0045: Consider the product of two exponential numbers having the same base with positive exponents such as five cubed times five squared.

pg096_n0053: The answer is five times, which gives the exponent.
pg096_n0054: Thus, five is multiplied by itself five times.

pg116_n0020: Rationalisation of a denominator involves eliminating radicals from the denominator of a fraction.
pg116_n0021: This makes denominator, to be a rational number.
pg116_n0022: The procedure for rationalising the denominator are as follows:
pg116_n0024: item one. If the denominator is a single radical term, multiply the numerator and the denominator by the radical in the denominator.
pg116_n0025: For example, in rationalising the denominator of a over root b, multiplying both the numerator and denominator by root b as follow.
pg116_n0026: a over root b equals a over root b times root b over root b equals a root b over b
pg116_n0027: Therefore, a over root b equals a root b over b.
pg116_n0029: item two. If the denominator is a sum or difference of two radicals, change the sign connecting the two terms.
pg116_n0030: The resulting expression is called the rationalising factor, which is then multiplied in the numerator and the denominator.
pg116_n0031: For example, in rationalizing the denominator of one over root a plus root b, the rationalising factor is root a minus root b.
pg116_n0032: Multiply both the numerator and the denominator by root a minus root b as follows.
pg116_n0033: one over root a plus root b equals one over root a plus root b times root a minus root b over root a minus root b equals root a minus root b over a minus b
pg116_n0034: Therefore, one over root a plus root b equals root a minus root b over a minus b.

pg124_n0012: Some real life situations such as earthquakes, population growth, and levels of acid or alkali in liquids are associated with very large or very small numbers.
pg124_n0013: In such cases, describing such situations becomes difficult.
pg124_n0014: However the concept of logarithm has made such descriptions easy for an individual to understand the effects of their occurrences.
pg124_n0015: In this chapter, you will learn to write numbers in standard form and use laws of logarithms to solve problems.
pg124_n0016: The competencies developed will enable you to simplify and find solutions to complex expressions, solve problems related to exponential growth decay, and understand the science of earthquakes and the spread of diseases, and many other applications.

pg124_n0024: When a number is expressed in the form A times ten to the power n, where one is less than or equal to A and A is less than ten, and n is an integer, it is said to be in standard form or scientific notation or standard notation.
pg124_n0025: For instance, the following numbers are expressed in standard form:
pg124_n0029: two hundred ninety equals two point nine times one hundred equals two point nine times ten squared
pg124_n0032: twenty-nine equals two point nine times ten equals two point nine times ten to the first
pg124_n0035: two point nine equals two point nine times ten to the zeroth
pg124_n0038: zero point two nine equals two point nine times zero point one equals two point nine times ten to the power negative one
pg124_n0040: When writing numbers in standard form, the following must be considered:
pg124_n0044: For numbers between zero and one, move the decimal point towards right until a number between one and ten is obtained and the exponent of ten is negative.
pg124_n0047: For numbers greater than or equal to ten, move the decimal point left until the value is between one and ten, resulting in a positive exponent of ten.
pg124_n0050: The exponent of ten is determined by the number of places the decimal point is moved, either to the right or left.
pg125_n0007: For the numbers which are between one and less than ten, the exponent of ten is zero.
pg125_n0011: In multiplication of numbers in standard form, the exponents are added, while in division the exponents are subtracted.

pg128_n0006: When a number is expressed in power form, it is written as a base raised to an exponent.
pg128_n0007: For instance, if a equals b to the power of x, then ‘a’ is written in terms of base ‘b’ raised to an exponent ‘x’ or ‘x’ is the logarithm of a to base b.
pg128_n0009: The exponent x is the number that shows how many times a base is multiplied by itself to obtain a product.
pg128_n0010: Thus, x is called the logarithm of a to base b.
pg128_n0011: Symbolically, this is written as log base b of a equals x, where a is greater than zero, b is not equal to zero and b is not equal to one.
pg128_n0012: This notation is called logarithmic notation.
pg128_n0013: For instance, sixty-four in exponential form can be expressed as sixty-four equals two to the sixth power.
pg128_n0014: The exponent six is called the logarithm of sixty-four to base two, written as six equals log base two of sixty-four.
pg128_n0018: Roman numeral one: twenty-five equals five squared is written as two equals log base five of twenty-five.
pg128_n0020: Roman numeral two: one thousand equals ten cubed is written as three equals log base ten of one thousand.
pg128_n0022: Roman numeral three: zero point zero zero zero one equals ten to the power of negative four is written as negative four equals log base ten of zero point zero zero zero one.
pg128_n0024: Sixty-four equals four cubed is written as log base four of sixty-four equals three.
pg128_n0025: Sixty-four equals eight squared is written as log base eight of sixty-four equals two.
pg128_n0027: In general, a equals b to the power of x is written as x equals log base b of a, where a and b are positive real numbers and x is a real number, b not equal to zero and b not equal to one.
pg128_n0030: When expressing the logarithm of a number, make sure to specify the base to which it refers.

pg129_n0006: The following are some special cases on logarithms of numbers:
pg129_n0010: If log base a of a equals x, then a to the power of x equals a to the first power, which gives x equals one.
pg129_n0011: Therefore, log base a of a equals one.
pg129_n0012: Thus, log base ten of ten equals one, and log base two of two equals one.
pg129_n0015: If log base a of a to the power of n equals x, for a positive number a, then a to the power of x equals a to the power of n, which gives x equals n.
pg129_n0016: Therefore, log base a of a to the power of n equals n.
pg129_n0019: If a to the zeroth power equals one, then log base a of one equals zero.
pg129_n0020: Thus, logarithm of one to any base is zero.
pg129_n0024: Base ten logarithms are logarithms of numbers to base ten, also known as common logarithms.
pg129_n0025: The base ten is usually left out when writing common logarithms to base ten.
pg129_n0026: For instance, instead of writing log base ten of three hundred and fifteen it is simply written as log three hundred and fifteen.
pg129_n0027: In general, log base ten of x is written as log x.

pg146_n0018: A set is a collection of well defined objects with common and distinct features.
pg146_n0019: The objects in a set are called elements or members of the set.
pg146_n0020: The members of a set are usually separated by commas and enclosed within curly brackets.
pg146_n0021: For instance, if B is a set representing students in a class and John is a student in that class, then John is a member of set B or is an element of set B.
pg146_n0022: This relationship is denoted by the symbol belongs to, which means a member of or an element of.
pg146_n0023: That is, John belongs to B.
pg146_n0024: For example, if C equals curly bracket one, two, three curly bracket, then one belongs to C, two belongs to C, and three belongs to C, whereas five does not belong to C, five is not an element of C.
pg146_n0025: The number of distinct elements in set A is represented by n of A.
pg146_n0026: For example, if A equals curly bracket a, e, i, o, u curly bracket, then n of A equals five.

pg148_n0054: Sets can be categorised into different types based on the number and nature of their elements.
pg148_n0055: The categories include: finite, infinite, singleton, and empty sets.
pg148_n0059: A set is finite if it contains a countable number of elements.
pg148_n0060: For instance, A equals open brace a, b, c, d, e close brace is a finite set because its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0064: A set is infinite if it contains an uncountable number of elements.
pg148_n0065: When representing infinite sets, a few elements are listed followed by an ellipsis, to indicate that the list does not have an end.
pg148_n0066: For instance, A equals open brace 2, 4, 6, 8, and so on, close brace is an infinite set because the entire elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0070: An empty set is a set which has no elements.
pg148_n0071: It is also called a null or void set.
pg148_n0072: For instance, the set of prime numbers between 31 and 37 is an empty set because there is no prime number between 31 and 37.
pg148_n0073: An empty set is denoted by the symbol open brace close brace, or empty set symbol.
pg148_n0077: A singleton set is a set that contains only one element.
pg148_n0078: For instance, H equals open brace 2 close brace.
pg148_n0082: Two or more sets can be compared and classified as equivalent sets, equal sets or one is a subset of the other.
pg148_n0086: Two sets are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0087: Normally, the symbol equivalent to is used to denote equivalent.
pg148_n0088: For instance, set A equals open brace 2, 4, 6, 8 close brace and set B equals open brace a, b, c, d close brace are equivalent because they have equal number of elements.
pg148_n0089: That is, n of A equals n of B equals 4.
pg149_n0004: Generally, if n of A equals n of B, then the sets A and B are said to be equivalent.
pg149_n0005: That is, A is equivalent to B.

pg149_n0018: Two sets, A and B are said to be equal if they are equivalent and their members are exactly the same regardless of the arrangement or order.
pg149_n0019: For example, if A equals open brace 1, 2, 3, 4 close brace and B equals open brace 3, 1, 4, 2 close brace, then A equals B since all elements of A are elements of B and all elements of B are also elements of A.

pg153_n0025: Set operations are categorized into four types namely: union, intersection, complement, and set difference.
pg153_n0026: These operations involve identifying elements in each set and determining the number of elements involved.
pg153_n0030: The union of two or more sets is the set that contains all the elements of each set, without any repetition.
pg153_n0031: The union of sets is represented by the cup symbol, union.
pg153_n0032: Thus, A union B denotes that an element x belongs to A union B if and only if x is in A or x is in B or x is in both A and B.

pg192_n0028: The angles of elevation and depression
pg192_n0030: When observing an object, you can either observe it horizontally if the object and line of sight are at the same level.
pg192_n0031: Observing it downward if the observer is above the object and observing it upwards if the observer is below the observed object.
pg192_n0032: To experience these scenarios, engage in Activity eight point five.
pg192_n0035: Activity eight point five: Studying different angles formed when observing objects
pg192_n0039: At your place, choose an object to observe which is at the same level as your eyes.
pg192_n0040: For instance, a person whose height is the same as yours and you look at his eyes.
pg192_n0043: In the second scenario, observe an object which you need to look downward.
pg192_n0044: For instance, looking at a coin on the floor while standing.
pg193_n0006: In the third scenario, observe an object that is in a position that requires you to look upward.
pg193_n0007: For instance, looking at the top of the building.
pg193_n0010: Study and reflect on all three cases and discover features such as angles formed, and possibilities of determining distances between the observer and the objects without measurements.
pg193_n0013: Use the internet or other relevant sources to study and justify your observations and share your findings through visual diagrams.
pg193_n0015: In Activity eight point five, it can be deduced that when observing an object below or above the horizontal level, the line of sight forms an angle below or above.
pg193_n0016: An angle formed between a horizontal level and a line of sight when observing an object downward is called an angle of depression.
pg193_n0017: The angle formed by observing an object upward is called an angle of elevation.

It is important to understand rates and variations.
They help you understand how quantities change in relation to each other.
pg008_n0013_easy_read:
Some variables depend on each other.
This means that a change in one variable affects the other variables.
pg008_n0014_easy_read: Many real-life situations include these relationships.
pg008_n0015_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will:
- describe the ideas of rates and variations
- explain the types of variations
- solve problems about rates and variations
pg008_n0016_easy_read:
The skills you develop will help you solve real-life challenges, such as:
- finding shopping deals
- checking fuel efficiency
- predicting data trends in economics, science, engineering, and many other fields

pg012_n0037_easy_read:
Variation is a relationship between two quantities.
When one quantity changes, the other quantity changes in proportion.
pg012_n0038_easy_read: Variation helps us explore connections between two or more quantities.
pg012_n0039_easy_read:
The four basic types of variation are:
- direct
- inverse
- joint
- combined
pg013_n0005_easy_read:
Direct variation is a relationship between two variables.
In this relationship, one variable is a constant multiple of the other variable.
pg013_n0006_easy_read: In other words, if one variable increases or decreases, the other variable also changes in the same direction and in proportion.
pg013_n0008_easy_read: This type of variation helps us understand how a change in one variable affects another variable in direct proportion.
pg013_n0010_easy_read:
Do Activity one point three.
Explore how direct variation is used in real life.
pg013_n0012_easy_read:
If y is directly proportional to x, we write it as y is proportional to x.
The symbol is proportional to means "is proportional to."
pg013_n0013_easy_read:
The equation that connects x and y uses a proportionality constant k.
Replace the proportional to symbol with an equal sign.
Then the equation is y equals k x.
pg013_n0015_easy_read:
For example, if y varies directly as the square of x, then y is proportional to x squared.
The matching equation is y equals k x squared.
Here, k is the constant of proportionality.
pg013_n0017_easy_read:
Take any two pairs of quantities x and y, such as open parenthesis x one, y one close parenthesis and open parenthesis x two, y two close parenthesis.
Then we get two equations:
- y one equals k x one squared
- y two equals k x two squared
pg013_n0018_easy_read: This means that k equals y one over x one squared, equals y two over x two squared.
pg013_n0019_easy_read: So, x and y vary directly when the ratios of the values of y to the values of x are proportional.
pg013_n0021_easy_read: If x and y are in direct variation, then y equals k x.
pg013_n0022_easy_read:
The equation y equals k x makes a straight line that passes through the origin.
In this equation, k is the gradient, or slope, of the line.
pg013_n0023_easy_read: Figure one point one shows the relation y is proportional to x when k equals one.
pg013_n0025_easy_read: Figure one point one: Graph of the relation y is proportional to x
pg013_n0027_easy_read:
Figure one point one shows this:
If quantity x increases, quantity y also increases in proportion.
If quantity x decreases, quantity y also decreases in proportion.
The same idea also works the other way round.

pg026_n0009_easy_read: In fields like architecture, engineering, and design, exact measurements and patterns are very important.

pg026_n0011_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about postulates, proofs, and theorems about congruence. You will also learn about the congruence of triangles.
pg026_n0012_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you solve problems. For example, you can find the side lengths of figures without measuring them. You can also design and make objects with the same shape and size, such as worn-out parts.
pg026_n0017_easy_read: Without knowledge of congruence, industries would need more time to produce objects of the same shape and size.
pg026_n0021_easy_read: The word congruence comes from the Latin word congruentia. It means agree or fit together exactly.

pg079_n0069_easy_read: A quadratic equation is when a quadratic expression is equal to a specific value.

pg079_n0072_easy_read: The solutions of this equation are also called roots or zeros.
pg079_n0073_easy_read: There are several methods to solve quadratic equations: factorization, completing the square, and the general quadratic formula.

pg080_n0011_easy_read: Step two. Rewrite the quadratic expression a x squared plus b x plus c as a product of two linear factors.
pg080_n0013_easy_read: Step three. Set each factor equal to zero. Then solve for x.

Then either x plus a equals zero or x plus b equals zero, or both factors are zero.
pg080_n0018_easy_read: This is called the Zero factor theorem. It says: if a product of two or more factors is zero, then at least one factor must be zero.

pg124_n0024_easy_read: A number is in standard form when it is written as A times ten to the power of n. In this form, A is greater than or equal to one and less than ten, and n is an integer. Standard form is also called scientific notation or standard notation.

pg124_n0040_easy_read: When you write numbers in standard form, remember these points:
pg124_n0044_easy_read: For numbers between zero and one, move the decimal point to the right. Stop when the number is between one and ten. Then the exponent of ten is negative.
pg124_n0047_easy_read: For numbers that are ten or more, move the decimal point to the left. Stop when the number is between one and ten. Then the exponent of ten is positive.
pg124_n0050_easy_read: The exponent of ten depends on how many places you move the decimal point. You may move it to the right or to the left.
pg125_n0007_easy_read: For numbers from one to less than ten, the exponent of ten is zero.
pg125_n0011_easy_read: When you multiply numbers in standard form, add the exponents. When you divide numbers in standard form, subtract the exponents.

pg128_n0006_easy_read: A number in power form is written as a base with an exponent.
pg128_n0007_easy_read:
For example, if a equals b to the power of x,
then a is written with base b and exponent x.
Also, x is the logarithm of a to base b.
pg128_n0009_easy_read: The exponent x shows how many times the base is multiplied by itself to get the product.
pg128_n0010_easy_read: So, x is called the logarithm of a to base b.
pg128_n0011_easy_read:
This is written as log base b of a equals x.
Here, a is greater than zero, b is not equal to zero, and b is not equal to one.
pg128_n0012_easy_read: This way of writing is called logarithmic notation.
pg128_n0013_easy_read: For example, sixty-four in exponential form is sixty-four equals two to the sixth.
pg128_n0014_easy_read:
The exponent six is the logarithm of sixty-four to base two.
It is written as six equals log base two of sixty-four.
pg128_n0018_easy_read: Roman numeral one. Twenty-five equals five squared is written as two equals log base five of twenty-five.
pg128_n0020_easy_read: Roman numeral two. One thousand equals ten to the third is written as three equals log base ten of one thousand.
pg128_n0022_easy_read: Roman numeral three. Zero point zero zero zero one equals ten to the minus fourth is written as minus four equals log base ten of zero point zero zero zero one.
pg128_n0024_easy_read: Sixty-four equals four to the third is written as log base four of sixty-four equals three.
pg128_n0025_easy_read: Sixty-four equals eight squared is written as log base eight of sixty-four equals two.
pg128_n0027_easy_read:
In general, a equals b to the power of x is written as x equals log base b of a.
Here, a and b are positive real numbers, and x is a real number.
Also, b is not equal to zero and b is not equal to one.
pg128_n0030_easy_read: When you write the logarithm of a number, make sure you also write its base.

pg146_n0008_easy_read: Objects belong to different categories and have different characteristics. Sometimes it is hard to describe them and understand their nature.
pg146_n0009_easy_read: Understanding sets makes it easier to categorise and organise these objects by their nature.
pg146_n0010_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn: the concept of a set; different types of sets; operations with sets; how to show sets in Venn diagrams; how to find the number of elements in a set.
pg146_n0011_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you: simplify problems; categorise problems; analyse problems; generalise problems. These problems come from real-life situations. You will do this in a more systematic way.
pg146_n0014_easy_read: This means organising and categorising data with little or no knowledge of sets.
pg146_n0018_easy_read: A set is a collection of clearly defined objects with common and distinct features.
pg146_n0019_easy_read: The objects in a set are called elements or members of the set.
pg146_n0020_easy_read: The members of a set are usually separated by commas and put inside curly brackets.
pg146_n0021_easy_read: For example, B can be the set of students in a class. If John is a student in that class, then John is a member of set B. John is also an element of set B.
pg146_n0022_easy_read: This relationship is shown by the symbol belongs to. It means "a member of" or "an element of".
pg146_n0024_easy_read: For example, if C equals curly bracket one, two, three, curly bracket, then: one belongs to C; two belongs to C; three belongs to C. But five does not belong to C. This means five is not an element of C.
pg146_n0025_easy_read: The number of distinct elements in set A is written as n of A.
pg146_n0026_easy_read: For example, if A equals curly bracket a, e, i, o, u, curly bracket, then n of A equals five.

pg148_n0054_easy_read: Sets can be put into different types based on the number and kind of elements they have.
pg148_n0055_easy_read:
The types are:
- finite sets
- infinite sets
- singleton sets
- empty sets
pg148_n0059_easy_read: A set is finite if its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0060_easy_read: For example, A equals open brace a, b, c, d, e close brace is a finite set because its elements can be counted.
pg148_n0064_easy_read: A set is infinite if its elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0065_easy_read: To show an infinite set, people write a few elements and then an ellipsis, open parenthesis dot dot dot close parenthesis. This shows that the list does not end.
pg148_n0066_easy_read: For example, A equals open brace two, four, six, eight close brace is an infinite set because all its elements cannot be counted.
pg148_n0070_easy_read: An empty set is a set with no elements.
pg148_n0071_easy_read: An empty set is also called a null set or a void set.
pg148_n0072_easy_read: For example, the set of prime numbers between thirty-one and thirty-seven is an empty set because there is no prime number between thirty-one and thirty-seven.
pg148_n0073_easy_read: The symbol for an empty set is open brace close brace or O with a slash.
pg148_n0077_easy_read: A singleton set is a set with only one element.
pg148_n0078_easy_read: For example, H equals open brace two close brace.
pg148_n0082_easy_read:
You can compare two or more sets.
Then you can classify them as:
- equivalent sets
- equal sets
- one set is a subset of the other
pg148_n0086_easy_read: Two sets are equivalent if they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0087_easy_read: Usually, the symbol equivalent to means equivalent.
pg148_n0088_easy_read: For example, set A equals open brace two, four, six, eight close brace and set B equals open brace a, b, c, d close brace are equivalent because they have the same number of elements.
pg148_n0089_easy_read: That is, n of A equals n of B equals four.
pg149_n0004_easy_read: In general, if n of A equals n of B, the sets A and B are equivalent.
pg149_n0005_easy_read: This means A is equivalent to B.

pg149_n0019_easy_read: For example, if A equals open brace one, two, three, four close brace and B equals open brace three, one, four, two close brace, then A equals B. This is because every element of A is in B, and every element of B is in A.

pg150_n0032_easy_read: Set A is a subset of set B if every element of A is also an element of B.

B equals open brace a, b, c, d, e close brace

If A has fewer elements than B, A is called a proper subset of B.
We write it as A is a proper subset of B.
pg150_n0035_easy_read:
If A is a subset of B and the two sets are equal, A is called an improper subset of B.
We write it as A is a subset of or equal to B.

pg150_n0038_easy_read: So, a subset of a set can be either proper or improper.
